tooltip.title: Diagnostic synthesis
tooltip.markdown: Use a convergent pattern rather than any single laboratory result.

tooltip.title: Examination
tooltip.markdown: Gottron papules/sign, heliotrope, periungual erythema with capillary dilatation/dropout, ragged cuticles, shawl/V-sign, holster sign, scalp erythema/scale, mechanic’s hands, palmar papules, ulcers, calcinosis.

tooltip.title: Examination and testing
tooltip.markdown: Test neck flexors, deltoids/abductors, hip flexors/abductors/extensors, and functional tasks. Distinguish true weakness from pain, arthritis, deconditioning, neuropathy, and steroid myopathy.

tooltip.title: Supportive, not solitary
tooltip.markdown: CK, aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT; CBC/CMP; urinalysis when overlap disease is possible. Myositis panels may be false-positive or false-negative and should be reconciled with phenotype.

tooltip.title: Myositis protocol
tooltip.markdown: Bilateral thigh MRI with fluid-sensitive sequences can identify edema/fasciitis and guide a biopsy site. Use EMG or muscle biopsy when the diagnosis remains discordant or another myopathy is plausible.

tooltip.title: Clinical and histologic differential
tooltip.markdown: Cutaneous lupus, psoriasis, seborrheic/contact dermatitis, phototoxic/photoallergic eruption, lichen planus, antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion-body myositis, muscular dystrophy, drug-induced myopathy.

tooltip.title: Clinical frame
tooltip.markdown: A phenotype-driven rheum-derm framework. Confirm the cutaneous syndrome, define muscle involvement, identify organ-threatening disease, and use autoantibodies for prognosis rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.

tooltip.title: Core evaluation
tooltip.markdown: **Myositis-specific antibodies · Muscle · Malignancy · Lungs.** Add swallowing, cardiac, joint, and calcinosis assessment when clinically indicated.

tooltip.title: High-specificity findings
tooltip.markdown: **Gottron papules/sign** and **heliotrope eruption** are the highest-specificity findings. Also inspect scalp, photodistributed chest/back, lateral thighs, palms, oral mucosa, and nailfolds.

children.name: Do not let a normal CK close the case

tooltip.title: Muscle assessment
tooltip.markdown: Symmetric proximal weakness is typical, but clinically amyopathic or hypomyopathic disease exists. Aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT, MRI, EMG, or muscle biopsy may be needed when the examination and CK are discordant.

tooltip.title: Time-sensitive risk
tooltip.markdown: Treat **dyspnea, rapidly progressive respiratory symptoms, dysphagia/aspiration, severe weakness, myocarditis concern, cutaneous necrosis, or extensive ulceration** as urgent multidisciplinary problems.

tooltip.title: Skin biopsy limitation
tooltip.markdown: A skin biopsy can support an interface dermatitis but usually cannot reliably separate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus. Distribution, morphology, nailfolds, muscle findings, and systemic phenotype carry the distinction.

tooltip.title: Phenotype directs surveillance
tooltip.markdown: Autoantibodies refine risk; they do not replace complete organ assessment.

tooltip.title: Prognostic use
tooltip.markdown: **MDA5:** ulcerative/palmar phenotype, arthritis, clinically amyopathic disease, ILD/RP-ILD. **TIF1γ:** extensive skin disease and cancer association. **NXP2:** severe muscle disease, dysphagia, edema, calcinosis; adult cancer association. **Mi-2:** classic phenotype, generally favorable muscle response. **Antisynthetase:** ILD, arthritis, Raynaud, fever, mechanic’s hands.

tooltip.title: IMACS framework
tooltip.markdown: Risk-stratify by IIM subtype, autoantibody, age at onset, dysphagia, cutaneous necrosis/ulceration, and persistent disease activity. Complete age/sex-appropriate screening for everyone; add basic or enhanced screening according to risk.

tooltip.title: Do not rely on symptoms alone
tooltip.markdown: Obtain baseline PFTs and use HRCT liberally in high-risk IIM/DM phenotypes. Cancer-staging CT is not equivalent to a dedicated HRCT protocol.

tooltip.title: Urgent when progressive
tooltip.markdown: Ask about solids/liquids, nasal regurgitation, coughing with meals, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, and voice change. Use speech-language/swallow evaluation and nutrition support when indicated.

tooltip.title: Targeted evaluation
tooltip.markdown: Inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud, myocarditis/arrhythmia symptoms, edema, calcinosis, lipodystrophy (especially juvenile disease), gastrointestinal vasculopathy in children, and functional disability.

tooltip.title: Treat the dominant and dangerous domains
tooltip.markdown: Skin, muscle, lung, and swallowing activity can behave independently. Document each domain and avoid interpreting persistent damage as active inflammation.

tooltip.title: Every phenotype
tooltip.markdown: Photoprotection, topical anti-inflammatory therapy, vaccination/infection risk review, bone protection when glucocorticoids are used, exercise/rehabilitation when safe, pruritus/pain control, and objective activity measures.

tooltip.title: Steroid-sparing strategy
tooltip.markdown: Topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor for focal disease; methotrexate or mycophenolate are common systemic choices. IVIG and selected targeted/off-label therapies may be used for refractory disease after phenotype and safety review.

tooltip.title: Early systemic control
tooltip.markdown: Systemic glucocorticoids are commonly used for substantial weakness or organ threat, with early steroid-sparing therapy such as methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate. IVIG is particularly useful in selected severe or refractory disease, including dysphagia.

tooltip.title: Multidisciplinary emergency
tooltip.markdown: Coordinate rheumatology and pulmonology. Mycophenolate, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors, or JAK inhibition may be considered by phenotype and trajectory; rapidly progressive MDA5 disease often requires urgent combination therapy.

tooltip.title: Avoid false failure
tooltip.markdown: Track strength/function, enzymes, patient symptoms, CDASI activity/damage, PFT trends, imaging when indicated, swallowing, and toxicity. Slow-onset therapies need an adequate trial unless disease is worsening.
